question.text: At which points on the surface $z= 2\sin x -xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v\!=\! \langle 8, 2\pi, 2 \rangle?$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \]

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (2\sin x -xy) \\[5pt] &=2\cos x-y \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (2\sin x -xy) \\[5pt] &= -x \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

\[ \left\langle 2\cos x-y, \: -x, \: -1 \right\rangle \]

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $\langle 8, 2\pi, 2 \rangle .$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

\[ c \cdot \left \langle 2\cos x-y, \: -x, \: -1 \right \rangle = \langle 8, 2\pi, 2 \rangle. \]

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} 2c\cos x-cy = 8\\ -xc = 2\pi\\ -c = 2 \end{cases} \]

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

\[ -x(-2)=2\pi \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=\pi. \]

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi$ into the first equation, we have \[ 2(-2)\cos \pi-(-2)y = 8 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y=2. \]

Finally, substituting $x=\pi$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

\begin{align*} z &= 2\sin x -xy \\[3pt] &= 3\sin{\pi} - (\pi)(2) \\[3pt] &= -2\pi. \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v$ at $(\pi,2,-2\pi).$

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z =e^{\sin(x+y)}$ at the point $(0,0,1).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

\[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^{\sin(x+y)} \right) \\[5pt] &= e^{\sin(x+y)}\cos(x+y) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{\sin(x+y)}\right) \\[5pt] &= e^{\sin(x+y)}\cos(x+y) \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (0,0) &= e^{\sin(0+0)}\cos(0+0) = 1 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (0,0) &= e^{\sin(0+0)}\cos(0+0) = 1 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

\begin{align*} z - 1 &= (x-0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) + (y-0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= 1(x-0) + 1(y-0) \\[5pt] z - 1 &= x + y \\[5pt] -x -y + z -1 &= 0 \\[5pt] x + y - z + 1 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)}$ at the point $(1,1,-1,1).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

\[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)} \right) = e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)}\cdot \cos(x+2y+3z) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)} \right) = e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)} \cdot 2\cos(x+2y+3z) \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left(e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)} \right) =e^{\sin(x+2y+3z)} \cdot 3\cos(x+2y+3z) \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,1,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} (1,1,-1) &=e^{\sin(1+2(1)+3(-1))} \cdot \cos(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\[5pt] &=e^{\sin 0} \cdot \cos(0) \\[5pt] & = 1 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} (1,1,-1) &=e^{\sin(1+2(1)+3(-1))} \cdot 2\cos(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\[5pt] &=e^{\sin 0} \cdot 2\cos(0) \\[5pt] &= 2 \\[7pt] \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial z} (1,1,-1) &=e^{\sin(1+2(1)+3(-1))} \cdot 3\cos(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\[5pt] &=e^{\sin 0} \cdot 3\cos(0) \\[5pt] &=3 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

\begin{align*} w - 1 &= (x-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,1,-1) + (y-1)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,1,-1) + (z-(-1))\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(1,1,-1) \\[5pt] w - 1 &= 1(x-1) + 2(y-1) + 3(z+1) \\[5pt] w - 1 &= x+2y + 3z \\[5pt] -x - 2y - 3z + w -1&= 0 \\[5pt] x + 2y + 3z - w +1&= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w = z\ln(x^2 + y^2 + 1)$ at the point $(0,0,3,0).$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w = f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as \[ w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0). \]

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( z\ln(x^2 + y^2 + 1) \right) = \dfrac{2xz}{x^2 + y^2 + 1} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( z\ln(x^2 + y^2 + 1) \right) = \dfrac{2yz}{x^2 + y^2 + 1} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( z\ln(x^2 + y^2 + 1) \right) = \ln(x^2 + y^2 + 1) \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (0,0,3)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} (0,0,3) & = \dfrac{2(0)(3)}{0^2 + 0^2 + 1} = 0 \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} (0,0,3) & = \dfrac{2(0)(3)}{0^2 + 0^2 + 1} = 0\\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} (0,0,3) & = \ln(0^2 + 0^2 + 1) = 0 \end{align*}

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: \begin{align*} w - 0 & = (x - 0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0,3) + (y - 0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0,3) + (z - 3)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(0,0,3) \\[5pt] w &= 0x + 0y + 0(z - 3) \\[5pt] w & = 0 \end{align*}

question.text: At which point on the surface $z= x^2 + 2y^2 - 7$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{v} = \left\langle 6, -8, -1 \right\rangle?$
question.explanation:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as \[ z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), \] where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2 + 2y^2 - 7\right) = 2x \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(x^2 + 2y^2 - 7\right) = 4y \end{align*}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is \[ \left\langle 2x, \, 4y, \, -1 \right\rangle. \]

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $\left\langle 6, -8, -1 \right\rangle .$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have \[ c \cdot \left \langle 2x, \, 4y, \, -1 \right \rangle = \langle 6, -8, -1 \rangle. \]

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system: \[ \begin{cases} 2cx = 6\\[3pt] 4cy = -8\\[3pt] -c = -1 \end{cases} \]

From the third equation, we get $c = 1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain \[ 2(1)x = 6 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad x = 3. \]

And substituting $c = 1$ into the second equation, we have \[ 4(1)y = -8 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad y = -2. \]

Finally, substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ into our function, we get \begin{align*} z & = 3^2 + 2(-2)^2 - 7\\[3pt] & = 9 + 8 - 7\\[3pt] & = 10. \end{align*}

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf v$ at $\left(3, -2, 10 \right).$
